chapters.summary: Shaun Abreu, filling in for Finance Chair Lee, opens the hearing and acknowledges Councilmembers Phil Wong, Frank Morano, and others who have joined.
chapters.title: Majority Leader Abreu opens hearing and acknowledges members

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's Finance Committee hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm Majority Leader Shaun-Abreu, and I have the privilege of chairing today's committee hearing in place of Finance Chair Lee.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'd like to recognize that we have been joined by Councilmember Phil Wong and Councilmember Frank Morano.

chapters.summary: Abreu explains the pre-considered bill would require DOF to establish a temporary program resolving outstanding ECB judgments, with default judgments payable at base penalty without interest and adjudicated judgments at 75% of penalties. The program would last 90 days in FY2027 with a possible 90-day extension.
chapters.title: Abreu outlines the ECB Amnesty and Compliance Program bill

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Today, the committee will hold a public hearing on a pre-considered bill sponsored by Finance Chair Councilmember Lee by request of the Mayor.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The legislation would require the Commissioner of Finance to establish a temporary program to resolve certain outstanding judgments imposed by the Environmental Control Board, ECB.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Under the program, eligible judgments resulting from default decisions could be resolved by paying the underlying base penalty

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: without payment of any default penalties or accrued interest, and eligible judgments resulting from adjudications and findings of liability could be resolved by paying 75% of the imposed penalties without payment of accrued interest.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The program would last for 90 days during fiscal year 2027, and the commissioner would be able to extend it for an additional 90-day period.

chapters.summary: Abreu notes similar ECB amnesty programs were authorized in 2019, 2016, and 2021, collecting millions in outstanding debt, and states the committee wants to learn about prior results and how this program will increase collections and revenue.
chapters.title: Abreu references prior amnesty programs and hearing goals

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The council has authorized similar ECB amnesty programs in the past, including programs in 2019, 2016, and 2021, which resulted in the collection of millions of dollars in outstanding judgment debt.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We look forward to hearing more today about the results of those prior programs, as well as how this proposed program is expected to increase collections, generate revenue, and otherwise benefit the city.

chapters.summary: Abreu recognizes additional council members who joined, thanks Finance Division staff including Deputy Director Edev, Chief Economist Dimnakou, analysts, and counsel for preparing the hearing, then introduces DOF Commissioner Richard Lee and Deputy Commissioner Annette Hill.
chapters.title: Abreu acknowledges additional members and thanks Finance staff

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We've also been joined by Councilmember Selvena Brooks-Powers, Councilmember Narcisse, Deputy Speaker Williams.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Before we turn to testimony from the administration, I'd like to thank the staff of the Finance Division for their work in preparing for this hearing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Deputy Director Emrah Edev, Chief Economist Dilara Dimnakou, Analysts Michael Sherman and Owen Katowski, Chief Counsel Nick Connell, Senior Counsel Nadia Jean-Francois, and Committee Counsel Brian Sarfo.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We will now hear testimony from our presenters from the Department of Finance, Commissioner Richard Lee, Deputy Commissioner Annette Hill.

chapters.summary: Committee Counsel Brian Sarfo swears in Commissioner Richard Lee and Deputy Commissioner Annette Hill before they begin their testimony.
chapters.title: Committee counsel administers oath to DOF witnesses

utterances.text: I will now turn it over to Committee Counsel to administer the oath.

utterances.speaker: Brian Sarfo
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Brian Sarfo
utterances.text: Do you swear to tell the truth and nothing but the truth before this committee and council members?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee

chapters.summary: Commissioner Richard Lee introduces himself and Deputy Commissioner Annette Hill, and explains the ECB Amnesty and Compliance Program aims to encourage resolution of ECB violations, increase compliance, and collect fines in an area difficult for the city to enforce.
chapters.title: Commissioner Lee introduces ECB Amnesty Program goals

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Can you hear me okay?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Majority Leader Abreu, Deputy Speaker Williams, members of the Finance Committee, and members of the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: My name is Richard Lee, and I am the Commissioner of the New York City Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: I am joined today by Annette Hill, Deputy Commissioner of Customer Operations.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify today on the proposed ECB Amnesty and Compliance Program Authorization legislation.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: The goal of the ECB Amnesty and Compliance Program is to encourage the resolution of ECB violations to increase compliance and collect fines in an area that is difficult for the city to enforce.

chapters.summary: Lee explains ECB violations are issued by over a dozen city agencies covering offenses like dirty sidewalks, littering, failure to remove snow, and working without permits. Issuing agencies include DOB, DSNY, FDNY, DOT, NYPD, HPD, DOHMH, DCWP, and PARCS.
chapters.title: Lee describes ECB violation types and issuing agencies

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: As a result, Environmental Control Board or ECB violations are issued by more than a dozen city agencies and cover a wide range of offenses including dirty sidewalks, littering, failure to remove ice or snow,

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: working without a permit from the Department of Buildings, and many other quality of life and environmental issues.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Agencies that issue violations include DOB, DSNY, FDNY, DP, DOT, NYPD, HPD, DOHMH, DCWP, and PARCS.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Violation recipients are typically businesses and property owners, but other individuals may be issued violations if they have committed an offense.

chapters.summary: Lee describes how ECB debt is referred to DOF upon OATH docketing of unresolved violations, explains that violations go into judgment after 100 days, and outlines that amnesty participants would receive a 25% reduction with interest waived and must resolve any violations requiring correction.
chapters.title: Lee explains debt referral process and program mechanics

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: ECB debt is referred to the Department of Finance upon Oates'docketing of unresolved violations that have been adjudicated by Oates'ECB subdivision.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: The proposed amnesty program will incentivize resolution and payment by reducing fines for individuals who have violations in judgment.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Violations go into judgment when recipients do not pay or dispute them within 100 days generally.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Amnesty program participants would receive a 25% reduction in the violation amount and will have the interest waived.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: The program would require the resolution of any outstanding violations which require correction.

chapters.summary: Lee notes the program is budgeted at $25 million and modeled on prior programs, explains it is useful where the city lacks strong enforcement mechanisms unlike the boot-and-tow program, and states idling violations are excluded because recipients are typically logistics companies less in need of amnesty.
chapters.title: Lee on budget, enforcement comparison, and idling exclusion

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: The ECB Amnesty and Compliance Program was included in the adopted budget for $25 million and is modeled after previous programs administered by the Department of Finance over the past 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Such programs are particularly useful when the city does not have a strong mechanism for enforcement, unlike, for example, our boot and tow program for parking tickets, where customers must resolve their debt in order to recover a vehicle.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: The amnesty program will be open for 90 days with an option to extend to 180.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Please note that idling violations will not be eligible for amnesty to ensure that we continue to hold bad actors accountable when they pollute our streets.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Additionally, the main recipients of idling violations are logistics.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: companies who are less in need of amnesty.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Developing a broad and simple program is the best way to achieve significant participation and ultimately resolve more violations throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Thank you for your partnership and I look forward to taking your questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Commissioner.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how many outstanding ECB judgments are eligible and the total debt. Lee reports $573 million in potentially collectible debt and $744 million deemed uncollectible as of the start of FY2026.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about outstanding ECB debt amounts

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm going to ask a few set of questions before I turn it over to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How many outstanding ECB, before I do that, I'd like to acknowledge that we've been joined on Zoom by Chair Lee, Council Members Hudson and Sanchez.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Back to questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How many outstanding ECB judgments are currently eligible for the program, and what is the amount of debt outstanding that is associated with ECB violations?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So as of the beginning of fiscal year 2026, we identified $573 million in outstanding debt that is potentially collectible, with an additional $744 million that is currently deemed uncollectible.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks how much DOF expects to collect through the amnesty program in FY2027. Lee states the budgeted ECB collection target is $100.76 million, including $25 million from the amnesty program.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about expected FY27 collections from amnesty

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What amount of ECB judgment debt does DOF expect to collect during FY 2027 through the amnesty program?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So as of adoption, currently the budgeted ECB collection target is $100.76 million.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Including $25 million from this effort in the ECB amnesty program.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So that's inclusive of the $25 million from amnesty.

chapters.summary: Abreu notes the 2021 amnesty program brought in over $43 million but OMB only projects $25 million for this program. Lee says the $25 million is an initial projection that will be updated as results come in, working with OMB.
chapters.title: Abreu questions why OMB projects less than 2021 program

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: OMB's last preliminary plan included $25 million in fiscal 2027 as anticipated revenue from the amnesty program.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Considering the prior amnesty program brought over $43 million in additional revenues back in 2021, why do you think OMB expects less than the prior program revenues?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: The $25 million was a projection at the end of adoption.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: As we go through the program and see results and successes, we will update the budget as we get along through the rest of the year, working in conjunction with OMB.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks whether the amnesty will be available to building owners given many ECB violations relate to health and building maintenance. Lee says a large number of DOB-issued ECB violations will be eligible and the program aims to ensure better corrections.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about building owner eligibility

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Many ECB violations relate to health concerns associated with building maintenance.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Will this amnesty be available to our building owners?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: There will be a large number of ECB violations that are from DOB.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: The result of this ECB amnesty program is to ensure that we have better corrections and people are actually addressing their violations.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We want individuals to correct these violations.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: And this is...

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Is one way to do so.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Will it be available to all building owners?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: It should be available to the vast majority of building owners unless it is currently under OATS system and has been docketed to us.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: There are some instances that we at the OF don't actually get all the ECB violations.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: It might be because of some criminal activity or such.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about owners with long records of poor management and those in the city's Alternative Enforcement Program. Lee says DOF is in constant communication with sister agencies and only DOF-docketed OATH violations are eligible for the program.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about poor building management and AEP eligibility

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And what if they are owners who have a long record of poor building management?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Of poor building management?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: That's something we'll discuss with DOB as we roll out the program.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We are in constant communication with all of our agencies throughout this process and as we start beginning the rollout of this embassy program.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Would you do the same as well with buildings related?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: To the city's AEP or other enforcement programs?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Right now, AEP at its alternative enforcement program.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We are in constant communication with our sister agencies on the rollout of this program, and so we are going to be working with them to determine which one of the programs will be viable.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: It's only for DOF ECB docketed violations, right?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So that's what it comes down to.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: If it's an ECB docketed violation, it should be eligible for the program.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: If it is a docketed ECB violation and any other agency, it won't necessarily be part of this program.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We are only looking at DOF docketed violations from Oath.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks when DOF plans to implement the program once the bill is adopted. Lee and Deputy Commissioner Hill indicate the anticipated start date is the beginning of October 2026.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about implementation timeline

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: When does DOF plan to implement the program within the year once the current amnesty bill is adopted?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We are currently working on this right now, and I think our anticipated date, Deputy Commissioner Hill?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: October, beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Of this year, correct.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'll turn it over to my colleague, Councilmember Morano, followed by Wong.

chapters.summary: Morano raises a fairness concern: one business owner pays a $1,000 violation while another waits and pays $750 under amnesty. Lee acknowledges the tension but says the goal is getting people into compliance, noting the program is run sparingly with no guarantee of future amnesties.
chapters.title: Morano questions fairness of amnesty for those who paid on time

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Thank you, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Commissioner, it's good to see you again.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: We've definitely missed you on this side of City Hall, most of the time.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I know you're somebody who takes these issues seriously, like the ones that we're looking at in this bill.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: I want to start with the basic fairness question.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Suppose two Staten Island small business owners get the same $1,000 violation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: One pays the $1,000 because that's what the law requires.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: The other doesn't pay, waits long enough, and under this program could potentially pay $750 and have the interest waived.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: What do I tell the first guy?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Well, there are going to be respondents in that situation.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: And that's why we're trying to strike a balance between that.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We want to ensure that those unanswered violations do become in compliance.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So that is the primary goal of this.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We're going to have better outcomes for the city if more people are in compliance with any judgments that they might have.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: How do we provide a second chance without sending the message that the financially smart thing to do is just to wait City Hall out?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So this program, again, isn't a program that we run normally or regularly.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We come to the city council for authorization of such.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: There's also no guarantee we will have another ECB-MDC program in the future.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So I would say that this is a program that we administer sparingly, but it is to ensure that we have better outcomes for individuals in the city.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: If people are addressing their outstanding violations, it is a better outcome.

chapters.summary: Morano questions whether the underlying problem is weak enforcement and asks what will prevent needing another amnesty in five years. Lee describes exploring policy changes including checking for ECB judgments when entities apply for permits and requiring cures before permit issuance.
chapters.title: Morano asks about strengthening enforcement infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: There was something in your testimony that really caught my attention.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: You say these programs are particularly useful where the city doesn't have a strong mechanism for enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Isn't that really the underlying problem here?

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: Don't we need to look at a stronger enforcement infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: That is one of the things that we are exploring, ways that we can introduce legislation that might give us better tools in enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: And we're working with several of our sister agencies in order to identify ways that we could better enforce ECB violations through legislation.

utterances.speaker: Frank Morano
utterances.text: If you had a recommendation, obviously you're not necessarily a policymaker, but if you had a recommendation, what are we going to do differently after this program so we're not back here in five years passing another amnesty for exactly the same reasons?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So we are exploring a couple of different policy changes.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: I'll give you one for example.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We're

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: looking at convergences between those entities that are, let's say, going in for permits for one reason or another, and looking to see if they have an ECB judgment in existence.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: And so we're working on a policy with several agencies to say if there is an ECB violation in place, then we should...

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We should have those entities cure those before issuing a permit.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So we are looking at different ways that we can creatively enforce on the existing population.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thanks very much.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Wong, followed by Brooks Powers.

chapters.summary: Wong asks about the $573 million collectible and $744 million uncollectible debt figures and what the program fixes that current tools have not. Lee explains the program incentivizes respondents to cure violations and that DOF is working to convert some uncollectible debt to collectible.
chapters.title: Wong questions what the amnesty program actually fixes

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you, Minority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Question, Commissioner Lee.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: You mentioned that

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: The DOF has figures of $573 million in ECB debt that is collectible.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, and then you already written off another $744 million as uncollectible.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: And that is for this year?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes, as of now.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Can you explain this new amnesty program?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What are you fixing that your current tools have not been fixing?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I mean, do we have like another year from now, are we going to see the same two figures except with the numbers being different?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: But what are you fixing?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Because as I see it, there will still be uncollectible debt.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So are you closing that gap?

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: What are you trying to fix?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: It's addressing a number of different issues, right?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We're trying to get respondents to be responsive to their existing violations and cure them and pay the violation costs.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: There will be some in the uncollectible category that might come in and say, now, okay, we will comply.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: And so we are looking at different ways that we can convert some of these uncollectible fines into collectible, and which we do every once in a while when we get new information.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We find that a business had been deemed uncollectible after previous attempts to address their violations, and we find new information, we move it from the category of uncollectible to collectible.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: And so we're hoping that through not only this effort,

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: But the other efforts we're putting in place within the Department of Finance, they will be able to better collect into the future.

chapters.summary: Wong notes most constituents pay fines on time and asks why the city keeps rewarding those who don't. Lee says the program is an occasional opportunity to cure violations, not run every year, and aims for better outcomes for the city.
chapters.title: Wong asks why program rewards people who don't pay on time

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, I'm going to follow up with that.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Weekly, I deal with constituents with fines and penalties.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Now, most of my constituents pay their fines on time.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: So can you explain why we keep rewarding the people who don't pay on time, which seems that's what this is doing?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So it is an opportunity for individuals to cure their existing violations, right?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: And this is one opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: This is not a program that we run every year.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: It's a program that we come to the council for authorization because we want to use it.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We don't want to have a situation where we're running this program every single year.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: With that said, it will have better outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: People who have addressed their violations will likely be able to address their violations and have a better outcome for the city.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: And so that is what we're hoping to do.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, I have a follow-up?

chapters.summary: Wong raises awareness of defendants who default multiple times and asks whether the program addresses them. Lee says the program gives small businesses a chance to cure instances and is not differentiated by offender history.
chapters.title: Wong asks about repeat defaulters in the program

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of defendants that default multiple times, and it seemed to me your program is not.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Are you trying to fix those, or what are you addressing?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We're trying to fix those as well.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Those small businesses who haven't had the chance to or was unable to, this might be a way for them to cure their instances.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Phil Wong
utterances.text: I have round two.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Second round, no problem.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Brooks Powers.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Followed by Narcisse.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Councilmember Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks why respondents default and how many defaults are due to notices going to incorrect or outdated addresses. Lee explains defaults occur for various reasons including inability to pay, inability to identify respondents, and businesses going bankrupt.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about reasons for default and incorrect addresses

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Good morning, Commissioner, and thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I have a question for you.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Sometimes I want to know why people did not pay their bill.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So from the data you have right now,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: I want to know, the bill gives the most generous treatment to the false judgments, right?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Why did those response defaults in the first place?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And how many of those defaults do you attribute to a notice going to incorrect or outdated address?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So as indicated earlier, our current uncollectible docket is about $744 million.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee

chapters.summary: Abreu asks whether DOF has evaluated results of prior amnesty programs from 2009, 2016, and 2021. Lee says DOF has evaluated to some extent and offers to provide specific information.
chapters.title: Abreu asks about evaluation of prior amnesty programs

utterances.text: Of the judgments resolved through the program, how many were default judgments and how many were adjudicated judgments?

utterances.text: We have not tracked that, but we're happy to maybe go back and look at it.

utterances.text: I'm having a few questions on outreach.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How does DOF plan to notify the public that the amnesty program is available?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Would there be a similar coordinated project implementation outreach for this current program?

utterances.text: Yes, we will use all communication methods with

utterances.text: news outlets with all elected officials and outreach teams at the different and impacted agencies.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: To ensure that we have success in the program.

utterances.text: Will DOF provide assistance to respondents in determining whether their judgments are eligible for the program?

utterances.text: That is something we do for all of the customers that come in through the Department of Finance.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And at the moment, do you have a projected cost to notify the public of the program?

utterances.text: We don't have a projected cost.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We are all working internally with our budgeted figures.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Whenever you get that information, it will be great.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You can pass that along to the committee.

utterances.text: I will now go to the second round of questions.

utterances.text: One second.

chapters.summary: Councilmember Restler commends Commissioner Lee's responsiveness and advocates for a day fines model where fine amounts are tied to income levels, arguing it would improve both revenue collection and deterrence. Lee says DOF is open to discussing the idea.
chapters.title: Restler proposes day fines model tied to income levels

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm a little nervous to call you Chair Abreu, but I'll do it anyway.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We miss our finance chair, but thank you for stepping in, Majority Leader.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I just want to say, Commissioner, it's always good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We miss you very much.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: I miss you guys too.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I have to just say I appreciate how impressively responsive you are.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Whenever there's an issue with the Department of Finance, you pick up the phone, you call, you try to work through solutions with us.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know these last couple weeks have been bumpy, but I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: for your proactive and clear communication and your partnership.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I really just want to commend you for that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I'm grateful that we're moving forward on the amnesty program, and I think it's a noble thing and hopefully a way that we can generate some additional revenue for the city and help people get up to date on what they owe.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I've long been a big champion of the Day Finds model.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Which one?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The Day Finds model.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: That Councilmember Brannon and others, I think actually this started as a Corey Johnson idea, that Councilmember Brannon took over and I think I have the bill now, I should know, whatever.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Oath has always hated it and they've always claimed that it's very challenging.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So the premise of the idea is that

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: For some people who are extraordinarily wealthy, a modest fine is a rounding error, and they don't care, and they'll pay it 100 times over, and it doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And for some people who are extremely low income, a modest fine causes enormous difficulties in their lives.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And if we were to create a pilot that...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Looked at income levels to inform what people could pay, it might actually be helpful in the city consistently collecting the revenue that we're owed and us

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: setting fines at a level that might actually deter bad behavior and improve conditions around the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is this an idea that you've considered?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Have you looked at this legislation previously?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is it something you'd be open to exploring together?

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: So I have not specifically thought about this issue.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: I have heard about the programmatic model, but we're open to always discussing any new ideas that anybody in the council or anyone else might have on new policy ideas.

utterances.speaker: Richard Lee
utterances.text: We're always open to that.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Well, we would love to explore that with you together.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Othe's always kind of claimed over, I guess, multiple administrations, at least de Blasio and Adams, that it would be very challenging to...

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Confirm the income levels of the individuals, and that makes the implementation challenging.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We've suggested you would just affirm it yourself, what your income level is when you are paying.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we thought it would be, we really think this is an overdue idea.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: The amnesty approach is one approach.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: We think this is actually a more sustainable model that would work better to not just collect revenue, but to improve behavior and conditions around the city of New York.

utterances.text: We're happy to discuss.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you very much, and thank you, Chair, for the time.

utterances.text: Yeah.
